title: Measures of central tendency: mean, median and mode

videos.script: Somebody asks how long a Horta delivery takes. You have twelve times in front of you, and they want one number. {{question}} There are three honest ways to answer, and they give three different numbers. {{three}} The first shares the total out equally. Add up all the minutes, divide by twelve, and you get the mean: thirty-eight point nine six. {{mean}} The second lines the deliveries up from fastest to slowest and takes the one in the middle. That is the median: thirty-seven point two five. {{median}} The third asks which value turns up most often. That is the mode. For delivery times it finds nothing, because no two times are the same. For the number of items in a bag, it finds three. {{mode}} Each one answers a slightly different question. The mean answers "what if everyone got the same?". The median answers "what does the middle customer see?". The mode answers "what happens most?". {{questions}} In this lesson you compute all three by hand, then in a spreadsheet, and you meet the mistake almost everybody makes with averages of averages. {{averages}}
